title: Sunday in AD 150
hookLine: a teacher named Justin explains Christian worship to the emperor: readings, a sermon, prayers, bread and wine, and a collection for widows
last: EVERY HOMELAND FOREIGN, EVERY FOREIGN LAND HOME.

lines: NO SECRETS: HERE'S WHAT WE DO.
TODAY, WE WALK INTO THE ROOM.
cards: Rumors travel fast about people who meet behind closed doors. So a Christian teacher named Justin does something brave: he writes a defense of his faith and addresses it to the emperor himself.
Near the end, he stops arguing and simply describes what Christians do when they gather. No secret rites, nothing hidden. Just the order of a morning.
Tradition remembers him as Justin Martyr, and his description opens a window onto a Christian Sunday from a time when, as he complains, Christians were accused of things they never did.

teach.b: In paraphrase: on the day called Sunday, everyone in the cities or out in the country gathers in one place.
The memoirs of the apostles, his name for the gospel accounts, or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as time allows.
When the reader stops, the one presiding speaks, urging everyone to imitate these good things.

teach.h: STAND AND PRAY, THEN BREAD AND CUP.
teach.b: Then all stand together and pray. Bread is brought, and wine mixed with water.
The one presiding offers prayers and thanksgivings as well as he's able, and the people answer, Amen. Justin explains the word for the emperor: in Hebrew, he says, it means so be it.
The bread and cup are shared, and the deacons carry some to those who couldn't come. This food, Justin says, is called eucharistia, thanksgiving, and only the baptized share it. Then the collection.

teach.h: A COLLECTION FOR WIDOWS AND STRANGERS.
teach.b: Those with plenty give what they choose, and the one presiding uses it for orphans and widows, the sick, those in prison, and strangers passing through. Why Sunday?
Two reasons: it's the first day, when God began making the world out of darkness, and the day Jesus Christ rose from the dead. Readings, a sermon, standing to pray, bread and cup, Amen, an offering.
Churches today arrange the pieces differently, and share the bread and cup more or less often, but the pieces are recognizable. And notice where the collection goes. Not to the building.

how: Christian Sunday services can include readings from scripture, preaching, prayers and an offering; churches differ on how often they share communion.

o: a deacon who carried bread to the sick at home
the first emperor to welcome Christian worship
a teacher who told the emperor how Christians worship

s: Justin describes the bread and cup being carried to people who were absent
the deacons take a share to those who couldn't come.
early Christian worship was a secret rite nobody would describe
Justin describes it plainly, in a defense addressed to the emperor.
Justin says the collection paid for the meeting place
he says it helps orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners and strangers.

games.q: you're Justin, writing to an emperor who's heard dark rumors about Christian meetings. what do you do?
o: keep it vague so nothing can be used against you.
describe the gathering, step by step, plainly.
games.why: he lays it out: readings, sermon, prayer, bread and cup, Amen, and the collection.

practice: Picture that plain room: people from the city and from the fields, someone reading for as long as there's time, everyone standing to pray, bread and a cup going around, a few pieces wrapped up for someone sick at home.
Notice who's in the room, and who isn't, and who's being remembered. If you pray, join their Amen; if you don't, let the picture be strange and familiar at once.

wordCard.voice: Justin. The teacher whose description of Christian worship shows readings, a sermon, prayer, bread and cup, Amen, and a collection for people in need.

orig.note: Greek: thanksgiving. Justin says this is what the bread and cup are called.

carryVoice: Your line: on the day called sunday. The deacons didn't forget the ones who couldn't come. Day seven hundred fifty-eight, done.
